stem: Myofibrils are part of which structure?
rationale: \- The myofibrils of skeletal muscle consist of thick, myosin-based and thin, actin-based filaments.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview

stem: Sarcomeres are part of which structure?
rationale: Most muscle fiber cells are aligned so that their sarcomeres are in parallel register (Figure 50-1).
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE > The Sarcomere Is the Functional Unit of Muscle

stem: Myosin is found within which structure?
rationale: The predominant form of myosin in contractile tissues is myosin II, hereafter referred to simply as myosin, an asymmetric hexamer.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE > Actin & Myosin Account for 75% of the Protein Mass in Muscle

stem: Myosin acts on which substrate?
rationale: When skeletal muscle myosin is complexed to actin to form actomyosin complex, the complex exhibits ATPase activity.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE > Actin & Myosin Account for 75% of the Protein Mass in Muscle

stem: Tropomyosin is found within which structure?
rationale: Tropomyosin is present in all muscle and muscle-like structures.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE > Tropomyosin & the Troponins Are Key Components of the Thin Filaments in Striated Muscle

stem: Troponin is found within which structure?
rationale: Troponin is unique to striated muscle.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE > Tropomyosin & the Troponins Are Key Components of the Thin Filaments in Striated Muscle

stem: ADP is converted into which substance?
rationale: While hydrolysis of ATP ultimately powers the cycle, the release of ADP provides the immediate driver for the conformational change in S-1 that translates chemical energy into the mechanical power stroke.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > MUSCLE CONVERTS CHEMICAL ENERGY TO MECHANICAL ENERGY

stem: S-1 requires which substance?
rationale: While hydrolysis of ATP ultimately powers the cycle, the release of ADP provides the immediate driver for the conformational change in S-1 that translates chemical energy into the mechanical power stroke.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > MUSCLE CONVERTS CHEMICAL ENERGY TO MECHANICAL ENERGY

stem: Cardiac muscle requires which substance for contraction?
rationale: Cardiac muscle requires extracellular fluid Ca^{2+} for contraction.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > CONTRACTION IS ORCHESTRATED BY THE SECOND MESSENGER Ca 2+ > Regulation of Contraction in Cardiac Muscle Is Also Actin-Based

stem: Smooth muscle requires which substance for contraction?
rationale: Smooth muscle requires extracellular fluid Ca^{2+} for contraction.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > CONTRACTION IS ORCHESTRATED BY THE SECOND MESSENGER Ca 2+ > Regulation of Contraction in Cardiac Muscle Is Also Actin-Based

stem: In which structure are ion channels typically found?
rationale: Ion channels are important in skeletal muscle.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > CONTRACTION IS ORCHESTRATED BY THE SECOND MESSENGER Ca 2+ > Ca2+ Enters Cardiomyocytes via Ca2+ Channels & Leaves via the Na+-Ca2+ Exchanger & the Ca2+ ATPase

stem: What is the substrate that adenylyl kinase acts upon?
rationale: Adenylyl kinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of AMP to form ADP.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > MUSCLE CONTRACTION REQUIRES LARGE QUANTITIES OF ATP > Adenylyl Kinase Serves as a Reserve of Last Resort

stem: What substance is required by muscle for its function?
rationale: Contracting muscles have a high demand for oxygen.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > MUSCLE CONTRACTION REQUIRES LARGE QUANTITIES OF ATP > Under Aerobic Conditions, Muscle Generates ATP Mainly by Oxidative Phosphorylation

stem: What substance is stored in significant amounts in skeletal muscle?
rationale: Skeletal muscle contains large stores of glycogen in the sarcoplasm.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > MUSCLE CONTRACTION REQUIRES LARGE QUANTITIES OF ATP > Skeletal Muscle Contains Large Quantities of Glycogen

stem: In which structure is glycogen primarily stored?
rationale: Skeletal muscle contains large stores of glycogen in the sarcoplasm.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > MUSCLE CONTRACTION REQUIRES LARGE QUANTITIES OF ATP > Skeletal Muscle Contains Large Quantities of Glycogen

stem: Creatine phosphate is converted into which substance during muscle activity?
rationale: Creatine phosphate can be used to regenerate ATP from ADP.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > MUSCLE CONTRACTION REQUIRES LARGE QUANTITIES OF ATP > Creatine Phosphate Constitutes a Major Energy Reserve in Muscle

stem: AMP is converted into which substance by adenylyl kinase?
rationale: Adenylyl kinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of AMP to form ADP.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > MUSCLE CONTRACTION REQUIRES LARGE QUANTITIES OF ATP > Adenylyl Kinase Serves as a Reserve of Last Resort

stem: In which structure is myoglobin typically found?
rationale: Type I fibers contain myoglobin and mitochondria.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > SKELETAL MUSCLE CONTAINS SLOW (RED) & FAST (WHITE) TWITCH FIBERS

stem: In which structure are mitochondria typically found?
rationale: Type II fibers lack myoglobin and contain few mitochondria.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > SKELETAL MUSCLE CONTAINS SLOW (RED) & FAST (WHITE) TWITCH FIBERS

stem: What is a recognized cause of dilated cardiomyopathy?
rationale: Mutations in the gene that encodes dystrophin have been implicated in dilated cardiomyopathy.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > SKELETAL MUSCLE CONTAINS SLOW (RED) & FAST (WHITE) TWITCH FIBERS > Mutations in the Gene Encoding Dystrophin Cause Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
rationale: Mutations in the gene that encodes dystrophin cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > SKELETAL MUSCLE CONTAINS SLOW (RED) & FAST (WHITE) TWITCH FIBERS > Mutations in the Gene Encoding Dystrophin Cause Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of Becker muscular dystrophy?
rationale: Mutations in the gene that encodes dystrophin cause Becker muscular dystrophy.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > SKELETAL MUSCLE CONTAINS SLOW (RED) & FAST (WHITE) TWITCH FIBERS > Mutations in the Gene Encoding Dystrophin Cause Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy?
rationale: Mutations in genes encoding polypeptide components of the sarcoglycan complex are responsible for certain other congenital forms of muscular dystrophy such as limb-girdle.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > SKELETAL MUSCLE CONTAINS SLOW (RED) & FAST (WHITE) TWITCH FIBERS > Mutations in the Gene Encoding Dystrophin Cause Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

stem: In which structure is sarcoglycan found?
rationale: The sarcoglycan complex is formed only in striated muscle.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > SKELETAL MUSCLE CONTAINS SLOW (RED) & FAST (WHITE) TWITCH FIBERS > Mutations in the Gene Encoding Dystrophin Cause Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

stem: EDRF is converted into which substance?
rationale: EDRF was identified as nitrous oxide (NO).
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > SKELETAL MUSCLE CONTAINS SLOW (RED) & FAST (WHITE) TWITCH FIBERS > Nitric Oxide Relaxes the Smooth Muscle of Blood Vessels

stem: In which structure are actin filaments found?
rationale: Although actin filaments in nonmuscle cells are not organized as in muscle, they can still interact with myosin.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > THE CYTOSKELETON PERFORMS MULTIPLE CELLULAR FUNCTIONS > Nonmuscle Cells Contain Microfilaments Containing G-Actin

stem: In which structure is vimentin found?
rationale: Vimentin-like proteins are distributed in various mesenchymal cells.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > THE CYTOSKELETON PERFORMS MULTIPLE CELLULAR FUNCTIONS > Intermediate Filaments Differ From Microfilaments & Microtubules

stem: In which structure is desmin found?
rationale: Desmin is distributed in muscle.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > THE CYTOSKELETON PERFORMS MULTIPLE CELLULAR FUNCTIONS > Intermediate Filaments Differ From Microfilaments & Microtubules

stem: In which structure is peripherin found?
rationale: Peripherin is distributed in neurons.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > THE CYTOSKELETON PERFORMS MULTIPLE CELLULAR FUNCTIONS > Intermediate Filaments Differ From Microfilaments & Microtubules

stem: In which structure are neurofilaments found?
rationale: Neurofilaments are distributed in neurons.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > THE CYTOSKELETON PERFORMS MULTIPLE CELLULAR FUNCTIONS > Intermediate Filaments Differ From Microfilaments & Microtubules

stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of progeria?
rationale: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS, progeria) is caused by mutations in the LMNA gene. The LMNA gene encodes lamin A and lamin C.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > THE CYTOSKELETON PERFORMS MULTIPLE CELLULAR FUNCTIONS > Intermediate Filaments Differ From Microfilaments & Microtubules

stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of skin diseases?
rationale: A number of skin diseases, mainly characterized by blistering, are due to mutations in genes encoding various keratins. Two such disorders are epidermolysis bullosa simplex and epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > THE CYTOSKELETON PERFORMS MULTIPLE CELLULAR FUNCTIONS > Intermediate Filaments Differ From Microfilaments & Microtubules

stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of blistering?
rationale: A number of skin diseases, mainly characterized by blistering, are due to mutations in genes encoding various keratins. Two such disorders are epidermolysis bullosa simplex and epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview > THE CYTOSKELETON PERFORMS MULTIPLE CELLULAR FUNCTIONS > Intermediate Filaments Differ From Microfilaments & Microtubules

stem: Cytoskeleton is part of which structure?
rationale: Nonmuscle cells contain an internal network of fibers called the cytoskeleton that provides the mechanical apparatus needed to maintain and change cell shape, provide cell motility, phagocytosis, etc.
citation: chapter_50_muscle_and_the_cytoskeleton — Overview
